steps: Step 1, Name the six Gulf Cooperation Council states and their capitals: Bahrain (Manama), Kuwait (Kuwait City), Oman (Muscat), Qatar (Doha), Saudi Arabia (Riyadh) and the UAE (Abu Dhabi). The council was formed in 1981. Locate each on a map by the Arabian Gulf coast.

Step 2, Learn the UAE's seven emirates: Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, Ajman, Umm Al Quwain, Ras Al Khaimah and Fujairah. Fujairah lies mainly on the Gulf of Oman coast, while most of the others face the Arabian Gulf. The federation was formed on 2 December 1971.

Step 3, Explain resources. Oil and natural gas are the main exports of Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Before oil, pearls, fish and dates were key. Saudi Arabia is the largest state in area, about 2.15 million square kilometres.

Step 4, Trace the old trade with India. Monsoon winds carried dhows from the Gulf to India's west coast in summer and back again in winter. Gulf traders carried dates and pearls; Indian ports sent timber, spices, rice and cloth. This shows a long link.

Step 5, Write a model answer: 'Ports like Dubai and Doha grew because they are on a sheltered coast between Asia, Africa and Europe. Ships can load oil, gas and goods, so trade brings jobs to people from many countries.'
Step 6, Your turn: name two resources of the Gulf and one old trade good. Model answer: 'Oil and natural gas are two resources, and pearls were an old trade good sold to India and beyond by dhow.'

Step 1, Countries depend on each other. The UAE has little farmland, so it imports wheat and rice, and India exports rice. India imports crude oil from Gulf countries. A phone may use parts from several countries. This is called interdependence.

Step 2, Trace one product. Dates grown in the UAE are sold to India, and Indian tea and spices come back. Trade helps both because each country sells what it makes well and buys what it lacks. Write one such pair as a sentence.

Step 3, Show why resources need care. Suppose a dripping tap wastes 1 litre an hour. In a day that is 24 litres, and in a week 24 x 7 = 168 litres. Many Gulf countries make drinking water from sea water, which uses a lot of energy.

Step 4, Give sustainable actions. Reduce, reuse, recycle; switch off lights; plant trees; use solar energy. Dubai hosted the United Nations climate conference, COP28, from 30 November to 13 December 2023. Countries agreed that cutting emissions matters.
Step 5, Write a model answer: 'A family can protect resources by taking shorter showers and recycling paper. This saves water and trees, so there is enough for children in the future.'

Step 6, Your turn: give one way countries depend on each other and one way to save energy at school. Model answer: 'Gulf countries sell oil to India, and India sells rice. At school we can switch off fans when the room is empty.'

Step 1, Link climate to vegetation. Station A: January 26 C, July 27 C, rainfall 250 cm a year. Station B: January 15 C, July 35 C, rainfall 15 cm. A is hot and very wet, so tropical rainforest; B is very dry with hot summers, so desert vegetation such as cacti and date palm.

Step 2, Calculate the range of temperature. Station A: 27 - 26 = 1 C. Station B: 35 - 15 = 20 C. A small range with heavy rain suggests an equatorial forest, like the Amazon or Congo basin. A large range with little rain fits a desert.

Step 3, Describe the forest and the desert. Rainforest trees are tall and evergreen, with dense layers and broad leaves. Desert plants have deep roots, thick stems for water and small leaves or spines. The UAE's ghaf tree survives in sandy dry land.

Step 4, Work out altitude. Temperature falls about 6.5 C for each 1,000 m. If a base town at sea level is 30 C, then at 3,000 m it is 30 - (3 x 6.5) = 10.5 C. So Himalayan slopes show forest zones changing with height.

Step 5, Write a model answer: 'Mangrove forests grow on salty tidal coasts, such as around Abu Dhabi and the Sundarbans, because their roots tolerate salt. They also protect the shore from waves and shelter fish.'

Step 6, Your turn: a region has 8 cm of rain a year and 40 C summers. Name its vegetation. Model answer: 'Hot desert vegetation, such as cactus or acacia, because water is scarce and plants must store water.'

Step 1, Begin with socialism in Russia. In 1917 the Tsar fell in February, and the Bolsheviks under Lenin took power in October. They aimed to end private ownership of factories and land. After 1928 Five Year Plans set targets for industry and forced collective farms.

Step 2, Explain Germany after the First World War. The Treaty of Versailles of 1919 made Germany accept blame and pay reparations. In 1923 prices soared so that people carried money in barrows. The Great Depression after 1929 left millions jobless.

Step 3, Read the data. The Nazi party won about 2.6 percent of the vote in 1928 and about 37.3 percent in July 1932, a rise of about 34.7 percentage points. Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933, and the Enabling Act of March 1933 gave him power to rule by decree.

Step 4, Show effects. Nazis banned other parties and spread a racist ideology. The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 stripped Jews of citizenship. About six million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust. The war began on 1 September 1939 with the invasion of Poland.

Step 5, Compare with a model answer: 'Both Soviet socialism and Nazism built one-party states with state control, but their aims differ. Socialism claimed to serve workers by common ownership, while Nazism rested on racial hatred and war.'

Step 6, Your turn: give two causes of Hitler's rise. Model answer: 'Economic collapse after 1929 caused anger and unemployment, and resentment of the Versailles Treaty let Nazis promise to restore German pride.'

Step 1, Define the idea. Nationalism links people who share a sense of belonging to one nation. After the French Revolution of 1789, ideas of a nation of citizens, a flag and a common law spread; the Napoleonic Code of 1804 gave equal legal rules in lands France controlled.

Step 2, Case one, Italy. Italy was split into states in the early 1800s. Cavour's diplomacy, Garibaldi's volunteers and Victor Emmanuel II of Sardinia-Piedmont brought most of it together in 1861, and Rome joined in 1870. From 1859 to 1870 is about 11 years of unification.

Step 3, Case two, Germany. Prussia under Bismarck won wars with Denmark in 1864, Austria in 1866 and France in 1870 to 1871. The German Empire was proclaimed at Versailles on 18 January 1871. Here unity came through war and a strong army, not mainly through popular uprisings.

Step 4, Compare in a small table. Italy: patriotic volunteers, a kingdom, central role of one state. Germany: military victories, an empire, central role of Prussia. Both: a shared language and culture, growing middle-class support, and leaders who used nationalist feeling to build one state.

Step 5, Write a model answer: 'Nationalism shaped Europe because it created new states, but it also produced conflict in the Balkans where many groups claimed the same land. This tension helped cause the First World War in 1914.'

Step 6, Your turn: how did nationalism grow in India after 1919? Model answer: 'Anger at Jallianwala Bagh and the Rowlatt Act led to the Non-Cooperation Movement of 1920 to 1922, which united many groups against colonial rule.'

Step 1, Date the policy phases. Planning began with the first Five Year Plan in 1951, which stressed agriculture, and from 1956 the plans gave priority to public sector heavy industry. By 1991 a balance of payments crisis, with very low foreign exchange reserves, led to reforms.

Step 2, Explain the 1991 reforms. They are summarised as liberalisation (fewer licences), privatisation (smaller state role in some sectors) and globalisation (lower import duties, foreign investment). Model answer should state both gains and costs in a balanced way.

Step 3, Compute growth. If GDP rises from 1,000 to 1,060 units, growth is (1,060 - 1,000) / 1,000 x 100 = 6 percent. If population grows 1.5 percent, per capita income grows roughly 4.5 percent, which affects living standards.

Step 4, Read sector shares. Agriculture employs roughly 45 percent of workers but produces under 20 percent of output, so productivity per worker is low there. This gap explains why rural incomes lag and why shifting work to industry and services is a goal.

Step 5, Measure poverty. Head count ratio = poor / population x 100. If 220 million of 1,000 million live below the poverty line, the ratio is 22 percent. Compare using HDI as well, which includes health and education, not just income.

Step 6, Your turn: assess one effect of the 1991 reforms. Model answer: 'Services and exports grew faster because of openness, but inequality between regions and sectors persisted, so growth needs jobs and skills too.'

Step 1, Fitness has components: cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, flexibility and body composition. For a 16-year-old at 60 kg and 1.65 m, BMI is 60 / (1.65 x 1.65) = 60 / 2.7225 = 22.0. Adults use 18.5 to 24.9 as normal; teenagers are compared on age-based BMI charts.

Step 2, Set heart rate zones. Estimated maximum is 220 - 16 = 204 beats per minute. Moderate to vigorous training of 60 to 85 percent gives about 122 to 173 beats per minute. Count your pulse for 15 seconds after a run and multiply by 4.

Step 3, Apply the FITT idea. Frequency: 5 days a week. Intensity: 70 percent of maximum. Time: 30 to 45 minutes. Type: running, cycling and body-weight exercises. Young people are advised to get at least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity daily.

Step 4, Draw a weekly plan. Mon: 30 min jog. Tue: strength circuit with squats and push-ups. Wed: rest or stretching. Thu: interval run. Fri: swim or cycle. Sat: team game. Sun: walk. Add 8 to 10 hours of sleep and regular water.

Step 5, Track progress. Week 1 test: 1.6 km run in 11 minutes and 15 push-ups. After 8 weeks, record again: 9 minutes 30 seconds and 25 push-ups. That is 1.5 minutes faster and 10 more push-ups. Write what you changed and what helped.
Step 6, Your turn: a student of age 17 wants a heart-rate range of 60 to 85 percent. Model answer: 'Maximum is 203. Range is 0.60 x 203 = 122 to 0.85 x 203 = 173 beats per minute.'

Step 1, Define sports for all: opportunity for every person, whatever age, gender, ability or income, to take part. Children with special needs include those with visual, hearing, movement or learning differences. The Paralympics began in Rome in 1960.

Step 2, Plan a school sports day for 200 students, 12 of whom have disabilities. Offer three stations: wheelchair relay, goalball for visually impaired players, and sitting volleyball. Inclusive design offers modified rules so all play together.

Step 3, Check the venue. A ramp rising 0.5 m at a slope of 1 in 12 must be 0.5 x 12 = 6 m long. Also keep clear paths, shaded seating, drinking water and a quiet area. Provide large-print or audio instructions as needed.

Step 4, Plan a 45-minute session: warm-up 10 minutes, skill practice 20 minutes, small-sided game 10 minutes, cool-down 5 minutes. Total 10 + 20 + 10 + 5 = 45. Pair students of different abilities, using the same equipment with adapted rules.

Step 5, Write a model aim: 'Raise activity so every student reaches 60 minutes of movement on at least three days a week, tracked with a simple tally sheet. Review after 12 weeks and adjust equipment or rules where students are left out.'

Step 6, Your turn: suggest two ways to include a girls-only afternoon and a student using crutches. Model answer: 'Offer a girls session with female coaches, and give the crutch user roles such as scorer or a seated throwing game.'
